transcript:
[00:00] Samir Rao: Hey everyone, thanks for joining; I'm Samir from Redwood, AE on the account, with Leah our SE and Jordan on product. How's everyone doing?
[00:12] Maya Torres: Doing well, thanks. Big agenda for us today - we want to see how batching and the KV cache will affect cost and latency for our payments chat pipeline.
[00:25] Daniel Reed: Yeah, our main goal is predictable latency under bursts, and to knock down token costs if possible. We're evaluating hosted vs dedicated.
[00:35] Leah Kim: Great, we'll walk through Optimize recommendations: batching thresholds, prefix/KV caching strategies, and the cost model we use to estimate unit economics. There's a slide deck I just posted to the chat - link: https://redwood.app/decks/optimize-batching-kv.pdf
[00:50] Priya Singh: Quick note, we have regulatory constraints in EU and need SOC2+ISO controls. Also, our keys live in Hashicorp Vault right now.
[01:05] Alex Boyd: And encryption-at-rest + KMS integration is a hard requirement, plus audit logs for every inference.
[01:12] Samir Rao: Totally, we'll call out the Private/Dedicated options. Redwood supports customer KMS and audit logs; we'll include the SOC2 package in the follow-up.
[01:25] Leah Kim: Ok jumping in: first, batching. Our runtime does continuous batching with latency SLOs. For short chat messages (avg 60 tokens), we recommend target batch sizes of 8-16 on gpus with 8-16 max concurrency. That balances throughput and tail latency.
[01:45] Daniel Reed: How do you pick the batch size automatically?
[01:50] Leah Kim: It uses workload-aware heuristics: request interarrival distributions, sequence length distribution, and SLO constraints. You can set max latency SLO (e.g., 150ms p95) and the runtime will back off batching when latency climbs. There's also an explicit max batch cap.
[02:05] Priya Singh: We have a lot of short messages but occasional long context windows for dispute resolution (2-3k tokens). How does that affect batching and KV cache?
[02:15] Jordan Lee: Important question. Long contexts will increase per-token cost and reduce batch packing efficiency. For those flows we recommend separating routes: a low-latency short-message route optimized for batching + small KV cache, and a long-context route that increases max sequence and uses prefix caching aggressively.
[02:35] [02:40] Maya Torres: Prefix caching vs KV cache - clarify for us?
[02:42] Leah Kim: Sure: prefix caching stores recent prefix activations to skip recomputation for repeated prefixes (good for multi-turn chat where prompts share stems). KV cache is for key-value attention caches across tokens to avoid re-encoding earlier tokens when generating continuations — critical for long sequences. In Redwood Optimize we model both effects: prefix cache improves compute per-request, KV cache saves decoder compute during generation.
[03:05] Daniel Reed: Do you have numbers?
[03:07] Leah Kim: Yes - using our sample benchmarks: for a chat workload avg 60 tokens with 2-turn context, enabling prefix caching and batching (batch target 12) reduced gPU token compute by ~45% and lowered cost per 1k tokens by ~38% on our m40-equivalent test. With KV cache active and optimized quantization, long-context flows saw up to 60% reduction in per-request compute.
[03:35] Priya Singh: Those are promising. Are the savings linear with QPS?
[03:40] Jordan Lee: Not linear - caching benefits depend on repetition and cache hit rate; batching benefit depends on burstiness. We provide a cost model: total_cost = base_token_cost * (1 - cache_savings) / batching_efficiency_factor + infra_overhead. You can upload traces and we'll estimate hit rates.
[04:00] Alex Boyd: For security, where's the cache stored? Is any customer data kept on shared hosts?
[04:08] Leah Kim: By default, in hosted mode caches are in tenant-isolated memory; for Dedicated/Private we persist caches on customer-only hosts. KV caches are in-memory by design for performance, but we support persistence to customer-managed storage in Private deployments.
[04:25] Maya Torres: Good. What's the impact on cold starts and CPU/GPU memory?
[04:30] Leah Kim: Cache warms quickly for repetitive prefixes; cold starts will have normal latency until cache fills. Memory overhead depends on model size and cache window; we provide profiling tooling to estimate memory needs before you commit.
[04:45] [05:00] Daniel Reed: On pricing - how do you model cost per million requests?
[05:05] Samir Rao: We provided a spreadsheet earlier; key levers are token count, effective tokens after caching, batching efficiency, and whether you run Dedicated capacity (flat monthly) vs hosted (usage-based). We'll attach a tailored sheet that models their QPS, % multi-turn reuse, and long-context percentage.
[05:25] Priya Singh: For our dispute flows (~5% of traffic long context), do you recommend dedicated?
[05:30] Jordan Lee: If those long flows require consistent tail latency and you have predictable volume, Dedicated is worth it - plus it simplifies compliance. We often see customers do Hosted for the bulk (burst) and route critical long-context traffic to Dedicated or Private.
[05:48] Maya Torres: Any tradeoffs on quantization? We've tried 4-bit and saw some quality drop in edge cases.
[05:55] Leah Kim: We recommend model-specific quant profiles; Optimize can recommend per-route quantization where short-turn chat can use more aggressive quant (Q4) and dispute flows use int8 or fp16. The Optimize console shows expected quality delta from evals vs cost savings.
[06:15] [06:20] Daniel Reed: Can you run our evals? We'll share a prompt set.
[06:23] Samir Rao: Yes — send the prompt set and we'll run A/B evals with your accuracy metrics. Leah - can you note that?
[06:28] Leah Kim: Noted. Priya, please upload the eval set to the shared drive link I posted.
[06:34] Priya Singh: Will do.
[06:36] [07:00] Samir Rao: Walkthrough of the cost-model example: open the spreadsheet - row one is baseline tokens, row two is cache hit rate inputs, row three is batching efficiency. If you increase batch target from 4 to 12 we show a 25-40% cost swing depending on QPS.
[07:20] Maya Torres: Does that assume perfect packing? We frequently have small micro-bursts.
[07:25] Leah Kim: We simulate realistic arrival distributions; perfect packing is rare. Our model takes a burstiness parameter. For micro-bursts packing improves but some requests will see reduced batching; that's why we recommend setting latency SLOs so the runtime auto-falls back.
[07:45] Daniel Reed: About fallbacks - if the primary model is saturated, what's the behavior?
[07:50] Jordan Lee: Configurable - you can set automated fallback to cheaper quantized variants or a smaller context model. Redwood also supports region failover. All fallbacks are audited in the console.
[08:05] Alex Boyd: On audit logs - format and retention? We need at least 13 months for compliance.
[08:12] Samir Rao: We support configurable retention, S3 export hooks, and streaming to your SIEM. We'll include audit retention options in the SOC2 package.
[08:25] [08:40] Priya Singh: A couple of nitty-gritty: how do you measure KV cache hit rate?
[08:44] Leah Kim: We instrument per-token cache lookups and log hit/miss counts per route. In the Optimize console you can filter by route, model, and timeframe. We also show effective tokens saved.
[09:00] Daniel Reed: We have a policy where any PII must not be cached for more than 24 hours. Support that?
[09:05] Leah Kim: Yes, TTL per-route is configurable, and in Private you can disable persistence entirely.
[09:12] Maya Torres: Can we do selective caching - e.g., cache only system prompts but not user messages?
[09:16] Jordan Lee: Absolutely — routing rules let you tag tokens and only cache certain token classes. That's a common pattern to cache static system prompts.
[09:30] [10:00] Samir Rao: Ok let's do a quick live demo of the Optimize console - Leah, you want to share screen?
[10:05] Leah Kim: Sharing now. (screen) [10:12] Leah Kim: Here is the route view. On the left you see batching target, latency SLO, and cache TTL. Middle pane shows expected cost delta with current settings and a simulated QPS curve.
[10:25] Priya Singh: That simulated QPS curve - can we upload our real traces?
[10:28] Leah Kim: Yes - you can upload CSV traces; the simulator will replay and estimate cache hits and batching. I'll drop the upload link in chat.
[10:36] Daniel Reed: In the simulation, what is the assumed model architecture?
[10:39] Leah Kim: You pick the model variant; we expose performance profiles for each model in the catalog. For today I'm using rwd-7b-quant as an example.
[10:50] [12:00] Maya Torres: On memory footprint, that model's KV cache size per session?
[12:05] Leah Kim: Roughly linear with sequence length; for rwd-7b we estimate ~1.2GB per 1k tokens of KV cache per active generation. The console shows memory per-route and warns if it exceeds node capacity.
[12:25] Priya Singh: That seems high for many concurrent sessions.
[12:30] Jordan Lee: That's why we recommend splitting high-concurrency short flows from low-concurrency long flows. Also, prefix caching reduces need to replay earlier tokens which helps.
[12:45] [15:00] Daniel Reed: Let's talk numbers for our projected monthly traffic: 40M messages, avg 60 tokens, 5% long-context averaging 2k tokens, QPS peaks at 900. What ballpark savings could we expect?
[15:20] Leah Kim: If we assume 50% prefix reuse on short flows and batching efficiency ~12, we'd model roughly 35-45% reduction in effective token compute for short flows. Long-context flows with KV cache and less aggressive quant might see 40-55% improvements. Overall you'd likely see ~33% reduction in monthly inference spend vs naive hosted baseline. We'll put these into the tailored spreadsheet.
[15:50] Maya Torres: Sounds good. Any caveats?
[15:55] Leah Kim: Depends on real cache hit rates and your QPS distribution. We'll run an actual replay to get better numbers.
[16:05] [18:00] Samir Rao: Security question - SSO and RBAC integration?
[18:04] Alex Boyd: Yes, we need SAML + role-based restrictions for who can change rollout/fallback policies.
[18:10] Samir Rao: Redwood supports SAML SSO and granular RBAC in the Console; we'll include the admin roles doc.
[18:18] Priya Singh: Also data residency in EU - can we keep inference in eu-west-1?
[18:23] Leah Kim: Yes, you can pin routes to region. For Dedicated or Private you can enforce region-only nodes.
[18:35] Daniel Reed: Next steps from our side: share traces, eval prompts, and confirm budget for a 6-week POC.
[18:45] Samir Rao: From Redwood: send pricing, run a 2-hour benchmark, produce a tailored cost model, and run an A/B eval.
[19:00] Maya Torres: Timeline — can we get the benchmark run by end of week?
[19:03] Leah Kim: We'll try; we'll prioritize once we get the traces.
[19:12] [20:00] Samir Rao: Any final questions?
[20:05] Priya Singh: One more - do you support explicit TTL purge on KV cache after a model update?
[20:10] Leah Kim: Yes, cache invalidation hooks are available, and we integrate with rollout APIs to invalidate caches during canaries.
[20:20] Daniel Reed: Great. Thanks everyone.
[20:25] Maya Torres: Thanks, useful session. We'll follow up with materials.
[20:30] Samir Rao: Thanks all—action items noted.
